summary: The article reviews major blackouts from September 2023 to February 2025, including the Capital City Gridlock, Great Eastern Blackout, a European interconnected outage, a California renewable-integration blackout, and the Texas freeze. It argues that aging, underinvested infrastructure is the common thread and calls for investment in transmission upgrades, smart grids, renewables, storage and weather-proofing.
one_line: Analysis of five major blackouts from 2023 to 2025 arguing that aging grid infrastructure demands urgent investment in modernization, storage and resilience.
key_facts: The Great Eastern Blackout occurred on November 10, 2023, plunging over 50 million people into darkness across eight states, with financial losses in the billions.
Officials attributed the Great Eastern Blackout to an outdated grid system unable to cope with surges in demand.
The Capital City Gridlock occurred on September 15, 2023, leaving government buildings, monuments and the metropolitan business district without power for twenty-four hours.
Senator John McIntyre led a hearing finding that an outdated power station failed and the interconnected grid collapsed like dominoes in the Capital City Gridlock.
On January 8, 2024, a significant portion of the European grid disconnected, affecting millions across three countries; the trigger was a minor incident in a substation in Germany.
EU Energy Commissioner Sofia Márquez called for a review of the EU's cross-border energy policies, balancing interconnectivity with independent energy security.
On June 30, 2024, a blackout hit California during record heat waves; solar generation was at an all-time high but the grid could not cope after sunset, and load shedding ensued.
California Governor Emily Thomson pressed for accelerated battery storage installations and transmission line upgrades after the June 2024 blackout.
In the Texas freeze of February 2025, power plants and natural gas pipelines froze, rolling blackouts became extended outages, and lives were lost.
The Texas Legislature passed bills mandating weatherization upgrades and creating emergency response measures; Texas Senator Elena Suarez was among those involved.
The article recommends investing in upgraded transmission lines, smart grid technology, expanded renewable capacity and resilience against natural disasters, which would also create jobs.
The article asserts that the cost of inaction is far greater than the price of upgrades and modernization.
